title: Dermoscopic concepts predicted from non-dermoscopic photographs: genuine visibility or shortcut?
claim: Can a model predict the seven dermoscopic checklist criteria from Derm7pt's paired clinical photographs — where those criteria are by definition not visible — and if it can, does the ability survive controls that remove lesion-identity shortcuts?
notes: Annotation provenance undocumented: unknown whether checklist annotators saw the paired clinical photograph. A positive result would have two materially different explanations. Unblocked only by author correspondence.

title: Eight named characteristics, or three latent ones? Discriminant validity of the LIDC concept vocabulary
claim: In the radiologists' own ratings, do the eight LIDC semantic characteristics agree with themselves across readers more than they correlate with each other within a reader - and if not, how many distinct dimensions does a concept model that reports eight separate concept predictions actually have?
notes: MTMM requires independent measurement methods. LIDC released reads are from the unblinded phase after readers saw each others marks, and reader IDs are not stable across scans. Keystone error: verified that multiple opinions exist (true) rather than that they are independent measurement methods (false).

title: Two papers say Sybil's residual signal is the background, one of them names emphysema, and neither measured it
claim: Sybil is using emphysema, and it reads it in a way that survives a change of reconstruction kernel that moves the standard quantitative emphysema index by about ten percentage points.

title: Murray's cube law says how a branching tree should be built - ask whether the risk model is reading the lung's departure from it
claim: The model is using pulmonary vascular pruning - the loss of blood volume in vessels below 5 square millimetres in cross-section, and the shift in the branching exponent away from the cube law that accompanies it - not parenchymal destruction.

title: Cardiomegaly on a CT report is admitted gestalt - ask whether the model has quietly turned it into millilitres
claim: CT-CLIP's cardiomegaly detector is using absolute heart volume in millilitres, not heart size relative to the chest, which means it over-calls cardiomegaly in large patients and under-calls it in small ones.

title: Forensic anthropologists age a skeleton by its rib cartilage - ask whether an unguided CT model found the same clock
claim: The chest-CT age model is using calcified costal cartilage volume - the same structure a forensic anthropologist scores to age an unidentified body - rather than aortic calcification, vertebral bone density or emphysema.

title: Two papers say Sybil's residual is the background and name emphysema; neither measured the heart calcium sitting in the same scan
claim: Sybil is using coronary artery calcium: on nodule-free screening scans its risk score rises with the automated Agatston score, and it does so over and above quantitative emphysema and small-vessel blood volume.

title: CT-CLIP has two calcification labels - coronary and arterial - so it can be asked whether it localises calcium or just sees hyperdensity
claim: CT-CLIP is using coronary artery calcium as a localised quantity: its coronary-calcification score rises with automated coronary Agatston and is not merely a readout of total calcium load, because it separates from aortic-wall calcium in the same scan.

title: An abdominal foundation model predicts diabetes - ask whether it is quietly reading the fat in the liver
claim: Merlin is using hepatic steatosis: its diabetes score falls as mean liver attenuation falls, and liver attenuation mediates a measurable share of the diabetes signal independent of visceral fat.

title: Merlin predicts osteoporosis - ask whether it reads the density of the bone or the shape of a column that has begun to buckle
claim: Merlin is using vertebral wedge deformity - the Genant anterior-to-posterior height ratio - and it weights the thoracolumbar junction most, rather than reading uniform trabecular bone density.

title: An airway and its artery run together and should taper together - ask whether the model reads bronchiectasis as the broken ratio between the two
claim: CT-CLIP is using the bronchoarterial ratio - the airway widened relative to its accompanying artery - and not merely the absolute size of the airway.

title: The cirrhosis model may be reading the bumpiness of the liver's edge
claim: Merlin is using liver surface nodularity - the fine nodular irregularity of the hepatic capsule caused by regenerative nodules - as its image signature of cirrhosis.

title: The chest-CT model may see the heart by watching the airway splay
claim: CT-CLIP is using the subcarinal angle - the splaying of the carina caused by an enlarged left atrium - as part of how it detects cardiomegaly.

title: The model that 'predicts a blood count' may just be reading how bright the blood is
claim: The model is using the CT attenuation of the blood pool - the radiodensity of blood, which rises and falls with haematocrit - to flag anemia.

title: The emphysema call may read the shape of the holes, not just how many
claim: CT-CLIP is using the morphometric complexity of emphysema - the power-law size distribution of the low-attenuation clusters (few large coalesced holes versus many small ones) - not merely the fraction of lung below -950 HU.

title: The lung-cancer model may read the aorta as an ageing clock
